opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is honestly one of the most underrated uses of language models right now. Many people still treat them like a slightly better search engine, and that leaves a lot of value on the table.

The way I think about it is that the hardest part of getting into a new field usually isn't the material itself. It's that you don't know what you don't know. You don't know which papers matter, what the jargon means, which debates are live and which are settled, or what the experts take for granted. Historically the fix was having a mentor you could pester with dumb questions. LLMs are a surprisingly good approximation of that mentor. They're infinitely patient, available at 2am, and you never feel embarrassed asking something basic.

Concretely, a few things I find really useful.

**Use it as a tutor while you read.** When I'm reading a paper outside my area, I'll paste in a confusing section and ask it to explain it at my level, or ask "what's the intuition here?" or "why would anyone care about this result?" Getting unstuck in thirty seconds instead of giving up is a huge deal for momentum.

**Have it test your understanding.** Explain the concept back in your own words and ask it to poke holes. Or ask it to quiz you. Lots of people feel like they understand something and then can't reproduce it, and this is a cheap way to find that out.

**Ask for a map of the field.** Questions like "what are the main schools of thought here?", "what would a skeptic say?", and "what are the five things every grad student in this area knows?" A rough lay of the land, even if imperfect, makes everything else you read slot into place.

**Context matters a lot.** Tell it who you are, what you already know, and what you're trying to do. "I'm a software engineer who knows linear algebra but no neuroscience, explain this" gets you a much better answer than a bare question.

The big caveat is that you have to stay calibrated about where they're reliable. They're very good on well-established, widely discussed material. They get shakier on niche details, recent results, and specific citations, and they can be confidently wrong. So I treat them as a brilliant but occasionally bullshitting friend. They're great for building intuition and getting oriented. For anything load-bearing, I check it against the source.

I'd also warn against letting it do the thinking for you. If you just ask for the answer every time, you'll feel productive but won't build the underlying skill. The value comes from using it to make your own struggle more efficient, not to skip the struggle entirely.

But overall, if you're trying to pivot into something like AI safety from another field, I think it's an enormous accelerant. People who use these tools well can get up to speed noticeably faster than people who don't. It feels like a genuine superpower that most people aren't fully exploiting yet.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs help people get oriented, fill knowledge gaps, and get up to speed faster when entering a new field.

r002.rationale: It describes LLMs as useful tutors for newcomers, but does not state that they are better suited to junior-level than expert-level work.

r003.rationale: It warns that LLMs can be confidently wrong and recommends checking important claims, but does not invoke junior humans’ fallibility as a reason not to expect perfect reliability.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the places where LLMs are just enormously underrated, honestly. When I was getting into mech interp, the way you learned a field was you read a textbook or a bunch of papers, you got confused, you had no one to ask, and you either pushed through or gave up. And now you have this thing that's basically an infinitely patient tutor that knows roughly the undergrad-to-early-grad-level version of every field, and most people still aren't using it that way.

So concretely, what I'd do is: don't start by asking it to explain the field. Start by trying to do something, and use the model to unblock yourself. Pick a paper you want to understand, or a small project, and whenever you hit a term you don't know or a step that doesn't make sense, ask. "Why does this work?" "What's the intuition here?" "Give me a toy example." And crucially, push back. If the explanation doesn't land, say "I don't get it, try again, I'm confused about this specific bit." A human expert would get tired of this after the third time; the model doesn't.

The other thing I'd really recommend is asking it to quiz you, or explaining the concept back to it and asking it to tell you where you're wrong. Because the failure mode when you're learning from an LLM is that everything feels clear while you're reading, and then you close the tab and realize you can't reproduce any of it. Being forced to generate the explanation yourself is where most of the actual learning happens.

Now, the obvious caveat is that models are confidently wrong sometimes, and the more niche the field, the worse this gets. For mech interp specifically, they're decent on the foundations and noticeably worse on anything from the last year or so, and they'll sometimes make up papers. So my heuristic is: use it heavily for the stuff that's been around long enough to be in lots of textbooks and blog posts, and treat it as a lead-generator rather than an oracle for the cutting edge. Get the model to tell you which concepts matter and what to search for, then go read the primary source.

And I guess the meta point is that the bottleneck in learning a field was never really access to information, it was feedback loops. How quickly can you go from "I'm confused" to "I'm less confused"? LLMs shrink that loop from days to seconds. If you're a motivated person who's willing to actually engage rather than just passively read, I think you can get to a working understanding of a new area maybe three to five times faster than you could a few years ago. That's a pretty big deal, and I think people who aren't doing this are leaving a lot on the table.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs can act as patient tutors that help people get started in a field and learn much faster, identifying reduced barriers to entry as a strength.

r002.rationale: It describes LLMs as knowing roughly the undergrad-to-early-grad version of a field, while being worse on niche and cutting-edge work.

r003.rationale: The response notes that LLMs can be confidently wrong, but does not argue that junior humans’ fallibility makes perfect reliability an inappropriate standard for evaluating them.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re really useful for getting over the initial barrier of not knowing what anything means. When I’m new to a field, I often can’t follow an explanation because it assumes five other concepts I haven’t learned yet. With an LLM, I can keep asking, “What does that mean? Can you give me a concrete example? Why would someone care about this?” There’s no social cost to asking a really basic question for the fifth time.

The caveat is that this is also when you’re least equipped to spot a wrong answer. So I’d use it alongside something more trustworthy, like a textbook or a paper. Ask it to help unpack a passage, then check whether the explanation actually fits what you’re reading.

And I’d try to make it interactive. Rather than just asking for an overview and reading a fluent answer, explain your understanding back and ask where it breaks down. Try an exercise. Make a prediction. It’s very easy to mistake “that explanation felt clear” for “I now understand this.” The useful thing is having a patient partner for doing the work of learning.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs help people get past the initial barrier of not knowing a field’s concepts and terminology.

r002.rationale: It discusses using LLMs while learning, but does not say they are better suited to junior-level than expert-level work.

r003.rationale: It warns that newcomers are poorly equipped to spot wrong answers, but does not argue that junior humans’ fallibility makes perfect reliability an inappropriate standard for LLMs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re really useful for getting past the stage where you don’t even know what questions to ask. You can say, “I’m trying to understand this field. Here’s my background. What are the key ideas, and how do they fit together?” And then you can keep asking follow-up questions without worrying that you’re wasting somebody’s time.

But I’d distinguish getting oriented from knowing that something is true. If it gives you a really clear explanation, that can feel like understanding, even when the explanation is wrong or you couldn’t actually use it. So I’d try to make the process active: explain the idea back, ask it to test you, work through a concrete example. And once you’ve got enough of a map, go and read some actual source material.

The thing I’d be excited about is how much this lowers the cost of being confused. You can ask the embarrassingly basic question, get an answer, and then say, “No, I still don’t understand. What does that word mean?” That’s a pretty powerful way to start learning.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs help people get oriented in a new field and lower the cost of being confused, including asking basic questions.

r002.rationale: It discusses using LLMs to get started, but does not compare their suitability for junior-level versus expert-level work.

r003.rationale: It warns that LLM explanations can be wrong, but does not argue that junior humans’ fallibility makes perfect reliability an inappropriate standard for LLMs.
